lessons.title: Grammar Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar A

Read the following passage carefully. Underline the verbs and identify their tenses. Passage: 'Hazrat Asma (RA) courageously faced many challenges during the migration. She had prepared food and supplies for the Rasoolullah (SAW) and her father, Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique (RA), before they began their journey. While they were travelling through the desert, Hazrat Asma (RA) was continuously checking their provisions and ensuring their safety. She had already secured their food by tying it with her belt, earning her the title of Zaat-un-Nitaqain. Her steadfastness and bravery were evident as she faced each obstacle with unwavering faith.' faced — Simple Past. had prepared — Past Perfect (completed before they began). began — Simple Past. were travelling — Past Continuous (action in progress in the past). was checking — Past Continuous. ensuring — Present Participle (part of the continuous construction 'was checking and ensuring'). had secured — Past Perfect. tying — Gerund (after 'by': 'by tying'). earning — Present Participle (result clause). were — Simple Past (linking verb). faced — Simple Past.

Grammar B

MODEL REWRITE (simple present): Hazrat Asma (RA) courageously faces many challenges during the migration. She prepares food and supplies for the Rasoolullah (SAW) and her father, Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique (RA), before they begin their journey. While they travel through the desert, Hazrat Asma (RA) continuously checks their provisions and ensures their safety. She secures their food by tying it with her belt, earning her the title of Zaat-un-Nitaqain. Her steadfastness and bravery are evident as she faces each obstacle with unwavering faith.

Grammar C

Last year, I faced a difficult examination week (Simple Past). I had prepared (Past Perfect) all my lessons before the week began, but on the first morning I was feeling (Past Continuous) very nervous. While I was revising (Past Continuous) my notes, my friend encouraged me and helped me stay calm. I had finished (Past Perfect) two papers before I realized that my fear was fading. In the end, I completed (Simple Past) all my papers with confidence, and I learned that steady preparation and calm effort overcome fear. (Tenses used: Simple Past — faced, completed; Past Perfect — had prepared, had finished; Past Continuous — was feeling, was revising.) Grammar D (Gerunds, Infinitives and Participles)

Read the following sentences carefully. Identify whether the verbs in bold are gerunds, infinitives, or participles: 1. Preparing food for the journey was Hazrat Asma's (RA) responsibility. 2. Hazrat Asma (RA) decided to support her family during the migration. 3. She received the title of 'Zaat-un-Nitaqain' for tying the food with her belt. 4. Honoured by her resourcefulness, the Rasoolullah (SAW) praised her actions. 5. Hazrat Asma (RA) continued to help the needy throughout her life. 1. Preparing — gerund (the -ing form used as the subject, a noun). 2. to support — infinitive (to + base verb, after 'decided'). 3. tying — gerund (the -ing form after the preposition 'for'). 4. Honoured — past participle (used in the opening participial phrase describing the Rasoolullah (SAW) as honoured). 5. to help — infinitive (to + base verb, after 'continued'). Grammar E (Gerunds, Infinitives and Participles)

1. showing (gerund after 'for'). 2. preparing (gerund after 'by'). 3. being (gerund after 'for'). 4. Facing (present participle in the opening participial phrase; 'Having faced' is also acceptable). 5. to give (infinitive after 'chose'). Completed sentences: 1. Hazrat Asma (RA) was known for showing great courage. 2. She helped her father by preparing supplies for the journey. 3. The Rasoolullah (SAW) praised her for being resourceful. 4. Facing many challenges, Hazrat Asma (RA) remained steadfast in her faith. 5. She chose to give away her inherited garden to the poor.

Oral Communication Skills A

Scholar: Trust, courage, integrity and generosity. She kept a dangerous secret under violence, comforted her blind grandfather with kindness, and later sold her inherited garden for the poor. Today, the same values mean keeping promises, protecting confidences, caring for elders and giving generously — the mark of a trustworthy citizen in any age.

Oral Communication Skills B

Trust means being relied upon and not failing that reliance. Hazrat Asma (RA) was trusted with the travellers' food, their hiding place and their secret — and she never failed in any of them, even when Abu Jehl struck her. Her example shows that trustworthiness is proved under pressure, not in easy times. Responsibility follows trust: she prepared, carried and guarded with minute care, because other people's lives depended on her. In modern life, the same standard applies to students trusted with class duties, employees trusted with money or information, and friends trusted with confidences: keep the trust, even when it costs you something.

lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

Entrepreneurship is the process of starting, managing and growing a business venture: entrepreneurs identify opportunities, take calculated risks and bring innovative ideas to life, creating products or services to meet market demands. It is important today because it creates jobs, drives economic growth, solves problems and gives people — including women — financial independence and control over their own futures.

Pre-reading

In our country, women run boutiques, bakeries, catering services, schools and online stores; globally, famous women entrepreneurs lead fashion, technology and food businesses. The unit's own example is Hazrat Khadija (RA), a prominent businesswoman of Makkah. Challenges they may face, as the unit lists, include cultural expectations that women prioritise household duties, limited access to finance, education and networks, mobility restrictions, legal and institutional barriers in registering businesses, and a lack of support networks and mentors.

Pre-reading

Women entrepreneurs improve communities by creating jobs (especially for other women and youth), providing useful goods and services, and starting businesses that address local needs such as education, healthcare and access to resources. They also serve as role models who inspire younger generations, challenge gender stereotypes, promote gender equality, and bring innovation and problem-solving into community life.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Hazrat Khadija (RA) was one of the wealthiest individuals of her time and was known for her wisdom, integrity and leadership in managing a thriving trading business. She carefully expanded her trading ventures, conducting business across various regions, and her influence extended beyond her wealth — she became a symbol of empowerment for other women. Modern women entrepreneurs can apply the same qualities: wisdom in decision-making, integrity in dealings, leadership in managing a business, hard work, intelligence and strategic thinking, and the courage to expand carefully even when society expects otherwise. Her example shows that gender should not be a barrier to success.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Women-led businesses contribute to economic development by creating jobs, generating income and boosting productivity, which results in a more dynamic economy that benefits everyone. They often employ people from their own communities, providing job opportunities and reducing unemployment, especially for other women and youth. In rural areas this matters even more: women in handicrafts and artisanship create handmade products like jewellery, carpets and decorative items which they sell in local markets or export, and women in education and training centres run schools, training institutes and daycare centres that serve community needs — so business growth directly becomes local employment and development.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Mentorship and networking are critical because, unlike male entrepreneurs who have access to established business networks, women often struggle to find mentors or role models, and the absence of such support networks makes it harder to succeed in competitive markets. Mentorship programmes guide aspiring businesswomen in developing essential skills; microfinance institutions offer loans to start small businesses; and women's chambers of commerce provide platforms for female entrepreneurs to network and showcase their products. Together these systems give women finance, skills, contacts and confidence — the very resources the unit lists as often limited for women, particularly in rural areas.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

E-commerce plays a liberating role: with the rise of digital platforms, many women use technology to launch online businesses, sell products via social media or run tech startups. The growth of e-commerce and online platforms has given women more flexibility, allowing them to run businesses from their homes and bypass some of the mobility issues they face — restrictions on movement that limit their ability to meet clients, travel for business or access markets. Online selling thus lets a woman reach customers without facing the cultural and mobility barriers of physical travel.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The success of women entrepreneurs serves as a catalyst because women entrepreneurs serve as role models for other women: by witnessing women succeed in business, younger generations are inspired to pursue their ambitions. Hazrat Khadija (RA) herself is presented as an example that has inspired generations of women to pursue their entrepreneurial dreams regardless of societal expectations. Each successful woman entrepreneur proves that barriers can be overcome, and thereby encourages the next generation to try.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Women's entrepreneurship benefits the wider community, not only the women themselves: it creates jobs, fosters innovation and promotes gender equality. Many women entrepreneurs start businesses that address local issues such as education, healthcare or access to resources, creating a positive social impact and improving the quality of life in their communities. It can be leveraged by supporting such ventures — for example, encouraging women to open training centres and daycare centres for education, or health-related services — and by the Government and NGOs providing financial resources, training and market access, so that business success and community welfare grow together.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Limited access to loans directly blocks women from starting or expanding businesses: many women, particularly in rural areas, have limited access to financial resources, education and networks, and banks may be hesitant to offer loans to women, while business training programmes are not always readily available. This keeps ventures small, informal or impossible. More equitable opportunities can be provided through microfinance institutions offering small loans, mentorship and training programmes, women's chambers of commerce for networking, and Government and NGO support with financial resources, training and market access — creating a more inclusive and supportive environment for female entrepreneurs.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

When women participate in the economy as entrepreneurs, they challenge gender stereotypes and promote equality: their success encourages society to view women as capable leaders and decision-makers rather than only as homemakers. By taking control of their futures, challenging societal norms and becoming leaders in their communities, women entrepreneurs break traditional gender roles. The unit's benefits list makes the point explicitly: promoting gender equality happens when women's economic participation challenges stereotypes, and the role-model effect then inspires younger generations, gradually changing what society expects of women.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

By providing them with financial independence and leadership roles in their communities. — how does entrepreneurship help women challenge societal norms in Pakistan.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Reading and Critical Thinking C

Entrepreneurship is the process of starting, managing, and growing a business venture.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A

Distinguish between the connotative and denotative meanings of the following words using context clues from the text. Give the context clue, denotative meaning and connotative meaning for each: entrepreneur, empowerment, independence, barrier, success. entrepreneur — Context clue: 'Entrepreneurs are the individuals who identify opportunities, take calculated risks, and bring their innovative ideas to life.' Denotative: a person who starts and runs a business, taking financial risks. Connotative: bold, creative, self-reliant, a leader and problem-solver. — empowerment — Context clue: 'She became a symbol of empowerment for other women.' Denotative: the process of giving someone power, authority or confidence. Connotative: liberation, dignity, breaking free from limits imposed by society. — independence — Context clue: 'entrepreneurship offers more than just financial independence.' Denotative: the state of not depending on others; self-support. Connotative: freedom, control over one's own future, pride. — barrier — Context clue: 'gender should not be a barrier to success' and 'societal barriers'. Denotative: an obstacle that blocks progress. Connotative: unfair restriction, especially social or cultural rules that hold women back. — success — Context clue: 'many female entrepreneurs finding success through determination and innovation.' Denotative: achieving a desired aim. Connotative: recognition, respect, proof that hard work overcomes odds.

Vocabulary B

Fill in the blanks with the help of suitable proverbs given below: a. Actions speak louder than words. b. A stitch in time saves nine. c. The early bird catches the worm. d. Don't put all your eggs in one basket. e. You can't judge a book by its cover. 1. If you want to succeed, remember that Actions speak louder than words. 2. Let's start our work now because A stitch in time saves nine. 3. To be successful, start your day early because The early bird catches the worm. 4. To minimize risks, Don't put all your eggs in one basket when making important decisions. 5. When meeting someone new, remember that You can't judge a book by its cover.

Vocabulary C

Match the idioms in column A with the correct meanings in column

Column A: i. Break the ice; ii. Once in a blue moon; iii. A piece of cake; iv. Hit the nail on the head; v. Cost an arm and a leg. Column B: a. very rare; b. to do something exactly right; c. to be very expensive; d. something that is very easy; e. to make people feel more comfortable. i. Break the ice — e. to make people feel more comfortable. ii. Once in a blue moon — a. very rare. iii. A piece of cake — d. something that is very easy. iv. Hit the nail on the head — b. to do something exactly right. v. Cost an arm and a leg — c. to be very expensive.

Vocabulary D

Identify the idioms and proverbs in the following sentences from the provided text and explain their literal and figurative meanings: 1. Women entrepreneurs in Pakistan are making strides in various fields, despite having the odds stacked against them. 2. She carefully expanded her trading ventures, proving that slow and steady wins the race. 3. By becoming entrepreneurs, women are breaking new ground and paving the way for future generations. 4. Women, who face criticism from society, often rise above it and prove that actions speak louder than words. 5. Despite limited access to resources, women are showing that where there's a will, there's a way. 1. 'the odds stacked against them' — Idiom. Literal: the chances in a game are piled up against someone. Figurative: facing strong disadvantages and unfair difficulties (here, societal and financial barriers) yet still progressing ('making strides'). 2. 'slow and steady wins the race' — Proverb (from the tortoise and hare story). Literal: a slow, steady runner wins a race. Figurative: careful, patient, persistent effort succeeds better than hasty action — as Hazrat Khadija (RA) carefully expanded her ventures. 3. 'breaking new ground' and 'paving the way' — Idioms. Literal: breaking untouched soil; laying a road surface. Figurative: doing something never done before (women entering business), and making future progress easier for others (future generations). 4. 'rise above it' and 'actions speak louder than words' — Idiom and proverb. Literal: to rise physically above something; spoken words making a louder sound than actions. Figurative: to overcome criticism without being dragged down by it; what a person does matters more than what they claim. 5. 'where there's a will, there's a way' — Proverb. Literal: wherever determination exists, a road exists. Figurative: strong determination finds a solution despite limited resources.

Oral Communication Skills A

Present your group's findings and join a whole-class discussion on the challenges and successes of women entrepreneurs. Whole-class discussion point — the successes are real, but the challenges of paragraph 8 (cultural expectations, limited resources, mobility issues, legal barriers, lack of support networks) remain, and overcoming them needs the support systems of paragraphs 6 and 12 (Government and NGOs).

Oral Communication Skills B

Hazrat Khadija (RA) was a prominent businesswoman of Makkah who managed a thriving trading business with wisdom, integrity and leadership. In a male-dominated society, she carefully expanded her trading ventures across various regions, proving that hard work, intelligence and strategic thinking could overcome the barriers of her time. Her wealth never defined her alone: her influence extended beyond it, and she became a symbol of empowerment for other women. Her story inspires future generations because it shows that gender should not be a barrier to success, and that a woman's business can uplift her whole community — the same lesson modern Pakistani women repeat when they turn a home-based bakery, a boutique or an online store into jobs for others.

Oral Communication Skills C

Entrepreneur: 'Thank you for coming. My business has focused on creating opportunities for women and challenging societal norms.' Community Member 1: 'Your business has provided so many women with jobs, allowing them to support their families.' Oral Communication Skills D

Resilience — Modern women entrepreneurs in Pakistan have faced and overcome cultural, financial and mobility barriers by building support networks, connecting with other female entrepreneurs to share advice, encouragement and opportunities, and by using e-commerce to run businesses from home and bypass mobility issues. Leadership and responsibility — They employ people from their communities, address local needs in education and healthcare, and act as role models, showing responsibility not only for their own success but for the community's welfare. Handling challenges therefore means combining personal resilience (determination, innovation) with collective support (networks, mentorship, microfinance, Government and NGO programmes).

lessons.title: Writing Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills A

Hazrat Khadija (RA) was a prominent businesswoman of Makkah Mukarramah who managed a thriving trading business with wisdom, integrity and leadership. In a male-dominated society, she faced the challenge of proving that a woman could succeed in trade; she overcame it through hard work, intelligence and strategic thinking, carefully expanding her ventures across various regions. Her influence extended beyond her wealth: she became a symbol of empowerment for other women, showing that gender should not be a barrier to success. Her impact on her community was therefore twofold — economic, through trade and employment, and social, through the inspiration she gave to generations of women to pursue their entrepreneurial dreams regardless of societal expectations.

Writing Skills B

Hazrat Khadija (RA), a prominent businesswoman of Makkah Mukarramah, shows how one woman entrepreneur can transform her community. First, her business itself created economic activity: she managed a thriving trading business and carefully expanded it across regions. Second, she overcame the challenge of a male-dominated society through wisdom, integrity and strategic thinking — proof that gender need not limit success. Finally, her impact went beyond wealth: she became a symbol of empowerment, inspiring generations of women. lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

Morning routine — waking up and getting ready: 30 minutes; eating breakfast: 20 minutes. School — attending classes, lunch break. After school — lunch, homework, extracurricular activities (e.g., sports practice), free time (e.g., watching TV, playing video games), dinner. Evening routine — family time, reading or activities before sleeping, getting ready for bed, sleeping time. Reflection: I spend too much time on video games and too little time on homework and reading. I would like to spend more time on sports and reading. To manage my time better, I will follow Taseer's lesson: put the 'big rocks' first — schoolwork, chores and family — and keep games and free time for afterwards, using a daily schedule.

While-reading

Taseer was well known for his cheerful nature and kind-heartedness, and he was adored by all. These are his positive qualities — but despite them, he had one flaw: his time management. He was terribly weak in managing his time.

While-reading

His teachers were greatly concerned about him, and his parents were also perpetually worried — because he procrastinated, spent hours on video games, chatting and daydreaming while schoolwork and chores piled up, and always seemed to run out of time, leading to rushed assignments and incomplete tasks. Yet Taseer was not ready to change his ways at all.

While-reading

The jar represents Taseer and his time. The big rocks are the significant things in life — schoolwork, family and health. The pebbles are other priorities, like hobbies and friendships. The sand represents the small, trivial things. If you fill your time with the small stuff first, you will never have room for the important things; but if you prioritise the big rocks first, everything else will find its proper place. The grandfather also helped Taseer make a schedule, setting aside time for schoolwork, chores and family activities, with hobbies and relaxation only after the big tasks were completed.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Taseer wasted his time by procrastinating: he spent hours together engrossed in video games, chatting with friends and daydreaming, while his schoolwork and chores piled up. Despite his good intentions, he always seemed to run out of time, which led to rushed assignments and incomplete tasks.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Poor time management made Taseer rush his assignments and leave tasks incomplete, so his schoolwork suffered. It also worried his teachers greatly and his parents perpetually, and it cost him control: he felt stressed about deadlines and had less time for family and friends. After he learned to manage time, the reverse happened — his grades improved and he felt more in control and less stressed.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Taseer eagerly began by pouring the sand into the jar first, followed by the pebbles. When he tried to fit the big rocks in, they did not fit, and he frowned, puzzled. His grandfather then emptied the jar and methodically placed the large rocks inside first, added the pebbles (which fit in the spaces between the rocks), and finally poured the sand, which filled the gaps left by the pebbles — and everything fitted perfectly.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

His grandfather, a wise old man, noticed Taseer's struggle: his teachers were greatly concerned and his parents perpetually worried, yet Taseer was not ready to change his ways. The grandfather decided to impart a valuable lesson, specially invited Taseer to his house, and taught him through the jar experiment rather than a lecture — so that Taseer could see for himself why prioritising matters.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Accurate time management transformed Taseer's performance: with practice and determination, he felt more in control of his time and less stressed about deadlines, his grades improved, and he had more time to spend with family and friends. His parents were proud of his progress, his friends appreciated that he was more reliable, and his teacher asked him to share his secret — which he did by telling the story of the jar, rocks, pebbles and sand, inspiring his classmates to try the same approach. He became a master of time management and grew up successful and happy, always making time for what truly mattered.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Exposition: We learn that Taseer is cheerful and kind-hearted and adored by all, but terribly weak at managing time — he procrastinates over games, chatting and daydreaming while work piles up. This matters because the whole plot is the curing of this one flaw; without it there would be no lesson and no growth. Rising Action: The grandfather's invitation, the jar, and Taseer's failed attempt (sand first, rocks do not fit) build tension — the reader shares Taseer's puzzlement — and the grandfather's methodical refilling (rocks, then pebbles, then sand) is the turning point, because the visual proof makes the abstract lesson unforgettable. Climax: The crucial moment is the grandfather's explanation — 'this jar represents you and your time' — when Taseer understands that big rocks must come first; his perspective changes from 'I never have time' to 'I must choose what fills my time first'. Falling Action: Taseer follows a schedule (schoolwork, chores, family first; hobbies and relaxation afterwards), practises with determination, feels more in control, less stressed, and improves his grades. Resolution: Taseer shares the jar story with his class, inspires classmates, wins his parents' pride and friends' trust, and becomes a master of time management for life. He learns that prioritising important things brings a balanced, fulfilling life — the story's theme of responsibility, growth and the value of time.

Reading and Critical Thinking C

Fill in the plot development diagram, based on the questions in B. Exposition — Beginning: Taseer, cheerful and kind-hearted, is introduced, along with his setting (home, school) and his problem: terrible time management (procrastination, rushed and incomplete work). Rising Action — The grandfather notices his struggle, invites him, and shows the jar experiment; Taseer's failed filling builds tension towards the lesson. Climax — The point of highest dramatic tension and the major turning point: the grandfather explains that the jar is Taseer's time and the big rocks must go in first; Taseer's perspective changes. Falling Action — The point at which the climax leads to resolution: Taseer practises the schedule, improves his grades, feels in control, and shares the story with his class. Resolution — The end of the story: Taseer becomes a master of time management, enjoys better relationships and a balanced, fulfilling life, and his story becomes a cherished reminder of managing time wisely.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A

Explain the meanings of the highlighted words given below: 1. Taseer often found himself procrastinating. 2. He decided to impart a valuable lesson. 3. Taseer eagerly began by pouring the sand into the jar, followed by the pebbles. 4. His classmates listened intently, and many of them decided to try the same approach themselves. 5. With practice and determination, he started to see improvements. 6. Taseer's newfound time management skills had a positive impact on his relationships also. 1. procrastinating — delaying or putting off work that should be done (Taseer put off schoolwork for games and daydreaming). 2. impart — to give or communicate something, especially knowledge or a lesson (the grandfather gave Taseer the jar lesson). 3. eagerly — with keen interest and enthusiasm (Taseer began the jar task keenly). 4. intently — with close, fixed attention (his classmates listened with full concentration); approach — a way or method of doing something (the jar method of prioritising). 5. determination — firmness of purpose, not giving up (Taseer kept practising the schedule). 6. impact — a strong effect or influence (better time management improved his relationships).

Vocabulary B

engrossed — synonym: absorbed. Sentence: He was so absorbed in his book that he did not hear the bell. admirable — synonym: commendable. Sentence: Her commendable honesty won everyone's respect. frowned — synonym: scowled. Sentence: The teacher scowled at the noise in the classroom. amazement — synonym: astonishment. Sentence: To everyone's astonishment, everything fitted perfectly in the jar. allocated — synonym: assigned. Sentence: The teacher assigned time for each activity in the schedule. impact — synonym: effect. Sentence: Good time management had a positive effect on his grades. cherished — synonym: treasured. Sentence: Taseer's story became a treasured tale in the school.

Vocabulary C

Use a dictionary to change the following nouns to adjectives. The first one has been done for you: nature — natural. Words: management, presence, gratification, expression, lesson, progress, reaction, struggle. management — managerial (relating to management). presence — present (being in a place; also 'present' as an adjective of attendance). gratification — gratifying (giving pleasure or satisfaction). expression — expressive (showing feelings clearly). lesson — NOTE: 'lesson' has no standard adjective form of its own in English; it is used attributively instead, as in 'a lesson plan' or 'lesson time'. progress — progressive (moving forward, improving). reaction — reactive (responding to something; in chemistry, readily taking part in reactions). struggle — struggling (present-participle adjective, e.g. 'a struggling student'); the related adjective of effort is 'strenuous' (requiring great effort).

lessons.title: Grammar Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar A

1. but (contrast: I wanted to go for a walk, but it started raining). 2. and (both burger and pizza). 3. or (a choice: nihari or pasta, but not both). 4. so (result: he studied hard so he could pass the exam). 5. yet (contrast: they were tired yet kept working). All five are co-ordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).

Grammar B

1. because (subordinating: reason). 2. both...and (correlative: She likes both tea and juices in the morning). 3. because (subordinating: reason). 4. Although (subordinating: contrast — Although he was tired, he stayed up late). 5. Unless (subordinating: condition — Unless you work hard, you won't pass). 6. both...and (correlative: He is both intelligent and hardworking).

Grammar C

1. and (She likes tea and coffee). 2. and (He went to the store and bought some milk). 3. but (They played outside but it started raining — contrast). 4. so (It was late, so they decided to leave early — result). 5. and (She enjoys reading novels and watching video lectures). 6. or (He is not tall or short — within this exercise's word bank; the more formal form is 'nor': 'He is neither tall nor short'). 7. and (They will visit the museum and the zoo; 'or' would mean a choice between the two).

Grammar D

moreover — Taseer made a schedule; moreover, he followed it every day. meanwhile — While Taseer filled the jar with sand, his grandfather watched meanwhile with a smile. (Better: Meanwhile, his grandfather prepared to show him the correct method.) therefore — Taseer prioritised his big rocks; therefore, he finished his work on time. in addition — In addition to his schoolwork, Taseer set aside time for his family. furthermore — Time management reduced his stress; furthermore, it improved his grades and relationships.

Grammar E

Rewrite each sentence using a different conjunction to convey a similar meaning. Example given: He will go to the beach if the weather is nice. Rewrite: He will go to the beach provided that the weather is nice. Sentences: 1. She likes coffee, but she doesn't like tea. 2. They went for a walk because the weather was nice. 3. He, not only studies, but also, plays. 4. They went skiing since there was fresh snow on the slopes. 5. He is both a talented musician and skilled painter. 1. She likes coffee, whereas she doesn't like tea. (Or: She likes coffee; however, she doesn't like tea.) 2. They went for a walk as the weather was nice. (Or: They went for a walk since the weather was nice.) 3. He studies as well as plays. (Or: He plays in addition to studying.) 4. They went skiing because there was fresh snow on the slopes. (Or: They went skiing as there was fresh snow on the slopes.) 5. He is a talented musician as well as a skilled painter. (Or: He is not only a talented musician but also a skilled painter.)

Oral Communication Skills A

1. Without his grandfather's intervention, Taseer would likely have continued procrastinating — rushed assignments, incomplete tasks, worried teachers and parents, and growing stress — and might never have discovered a practical method for change, since he 'wasn't ready to change his ways at all' on his own. 2. lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Reading and Critical Thinking A

Write down the examples and the evidence supporting your inferences. The author views the pre-Islamic Arabs with admiration for their gifts, alongside sorrow for their age's decline. Evidence: the Arabs had wonderful memories and eloquence — at the yearly poetical fair at Ukaz, poets competed, and Hammad recited to Caliph Walid bin Yazid a hundred long poems for every letter of the alphabet; their poetry was so valued that the fair was a national event. At the same time, the author shows their age (the 5th-6th centuries) as one in which civilization was crumbling and society stood on the verge of chaos — which is why the coming of the Rasoolullah (SAW) and the revelation are presented as the end of that waiting and darkness.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Patriotism helps people work together in tough times because it gives them a shared love for the motherland and a willingness to sacrifice for it. In a flood or a pandemic, patriotic citizens volunteer, donate, follow safety rules, help neighbours, and support health workers and soldiers — just as the soldiers of 1965, 1971 and Kargil sacrificed for the country, ordinary citizens sacrifice comfort and time for the nation. The spirit of patriotism, which the unit calls a living spirit that inspires and guides a nation, turns individual effort into united national action, and Quaid-e-Azam's call — to be galvanized into a united and strong nation — applies exactly to such crises.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Initially, the poet is wandering lonely as a cloud when he suddenly sees the golden daffodils; he gazes and gazes in wonder, and the dancing flowers fill him with joy he does not yet fully understand ('I gazed — and gazed — but little thought / What wealth the show to me had brought'). Later, when he lies on his couch in a vacant or in pensive mood, the daffodils flash upon his inward eye — the bliss of solitude — and his heart fills with pleasure and dances with the daffodils. So the sight first lifts him from loneliness to joyful wonder, and later, in memory, it turns solitude itself into bliss.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Her contributions were essential to the migration's success: she prepared the food at her father's house, tied it with her own belt (earning the title Zaat-un-Nitaqain), and carried it nightly to the cave of Thawr with minute care, while guarding the secret of the travellers' whereabouts absolutely — even under Abu Jehl's violence. Without her support, the travellers could have starved in hiding or been discovered: without food they could not remain in the cave, and without her silence the searchers, tempted by huge bounties, could have found them. The migration might then have failed, with the gravest consequences for the Rasoolullah (SAW) and Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA). Her courage, resourcefulness and trustworthiness therefore directly protected the Hijrat.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Beyond economic growth, entrepreneurship influences society by creating jobs (especially for other women and youth), empowering women with financial independence and leadership roles, challenging gender stereotypes and promoting gender equality, fostering innovation and problem-solving, developing communities (businesses addressing education, healthcare and access to resources), and inspiring future generations as role models. As the unit concludes, by supporting women's entrepreneurship and addressing the barriers they face, society can unlock the potential of half its population, paving the way for a brighter future — an influence far wider than income alone.

Writing Skills A

A student in our class, Bilal, comes from a farming village, while his classmate Sarah's family recently moved from another province and speaks a different language at home. At first they misunderstood each other, but Bilal showed respect by listening patiently when Sarah spoke, learning a few words of her language, and inviting her to join his study group. This respect changed their relationship: Sarah felt welcome instead of isolated, Bilal learned about a new culture, and both began to help each other — Bilal with mathematics, Sarah with English. Their respect built understanding, just as Hazrat Asma (RA) showed respect for her grandfather despite their differences of faith, and proved that respect for difference strengthens rather than weakens a relationship.

Writing Skills B

In a small town, a schoolgirl named Ayesha noticed that the poorest children in her street were charged extra by a shopkeeper for the same notebooks. She decided to fight for justice, but the obstacles were real: the shopkeeper threatened to refuse her family service, and some neighbours told her to stay quiet. lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

The qualities important for integrity and resilience are self-control (keeping your head when others lose theirs), honesty (not dealing in lies even when lied about), patience (waiting without being tired by waiting), humility (not looking too good or talking too wise), courage (risking and losing and starting again without complaint), and perseverance (holding on when there is nothing left except the Will). Predicted themes of 'If': patience, self-trust balanced with humility, balanced attitudes to dreams and thoughts, treating Triumph and Disaster alike, resilience after loss, integrity among crowds and kings, and filling each minute with purposeful effort — the poem's own portrait of becoming a Man.

While-reading

I will handle failure as the poem teaches: meet Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same — neither letting success make me proud nor letting failure break me. If I lose, I will start again at my beginnings and never breathe a word about my loss; if the things I gave my life to are broken, I will stoop and build them up again with worn-out tools. Failure, in the poem's view, is not an end but a test of whether I can hold on when there is nothing left except the Will that says, 'Hold on!'

While-reading

I will celebrate success with the same balance the poem demands: by not letting triumph become my master, by keeping my virtue when talking with crowds and keeping the common touch when walking with Kings, and by letting all men count with me but none too much. True celebration, in the poem's terms, is quiet and steady — filling the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds' worth of distance run — rather than boasting, because Triumph is an impostor just like Disaster, and both must be treated the same.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

One should keep one's head when all about are losing theirs and blaming it on you, and trust oneself when all men doubt you, but make allowance for their doubting too. That is, respond to criticism and blame with calm self-control and self-trust, without anger and without dismissing the critics entirely — allow that their doubt may have some ground, but do not lose your head because of it.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The poem emphasizes balanced self-trust: trust yourself when all men doubt you, but make allowance for their doubting too. It is not stubborn pride — the same stanza warns against looking too good or talking too wise, and against giving way to hating when hated or dealing in lies when lied about. The quality is confident humility: firm in oneself, fair to others.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Dream, but do not make dreams your master; think, but do not make thoughts your aim. Aspirations are vital, but they must stay under your control: a person should pursue goals while remaining grounded and realistic, not letting dreams rule his life or letting thought replace action. Dreams guide; they must not enslave.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

If you can bear to hear the truth you have spoken twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools, and watch the things you gave your life to, broken, and stoop and build them up with worn-out tools — that is the poem's answer: endure misrepresentation without bitterness, and rebuild patiently even with poor tools. Likewise, if you make one heap of all your winnings, risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss, and lose, start again at your beginnings and never breathe a word about your loss — accept loss without complaint and begin again.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Resilience means rebuilding after ruin and starting again after total loss: stoop and build up with worn-out tools what was broken, and after losing everything on one turn, start again at your beginnings without a word about the loss. It also means forcing heart, nerve and sinew to serve your turn long after they are gone, and holding on when there is nothing left in you except the Will which says, 'Hold on!' Resilience, for Kipling, is not a single brave act but steady endurance powered by will.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Persist by forcing your heart, nerve and sinew to serve your turn long after they are gone, and holding on when there is nothing in you except the Will which says to them: 'Hold on!' Persistence also means waiting without being tired by waiting, and filling the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds' worth of distance run — using every moment fully rather than surrendering to difficulty.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Integrity and humility mean: keep your virtue when talking with crowds, and keep the common touch when walking with Kings; let neither foes nor loving friends hurt you; let all men count with you, but none too much. Do not deal in lies when lied about, do not give way to hating when hated, and do not look too good or talk too wise. The reward of such a life, the poem says, is: 'Yours is the Earth and everything that's in it, and — which is more — you'll be a Man, my son!'

mcqs.q: According to the poem as explained in the notes, what should you do when all about you are losing their heads and blaming it on you?
options: Keep your head and stay calm
Lose your temper to prove your point

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A

Identify the figure of speech and write its type against each sentence: 1. The water was as cold as ice. 2. The car was moving as slowly as a snail. 3. The leaves waved goodbye as they fell from the tree. 4. The alarm clock screamed at me. 5. His temper was a volcano, ready to erupt. 6. Her laughter was a sweet symphony. 1. Simile (comparison using 'as': water as cold as ice). 2. Simile (comparison using 'as': car as slowly as a snail). 3. Personification (leaves are given the human action of waving goodbye). 4. Personification (the alarm clock is given the human action of screaming). 5. Metaphor (direct comparison without 'as'/'like': temper is a volcano). 6. Metaphor (direct comparison: laughter is a sweet symphony).

mcqs.q: 'The water was as cold as ice.' Which figure of speech is this?
mcqs.why: The notes identify this as a simile, a comparison using 'as': the water is compared with ice for coldness.

mcqs.q: 'The car was moving as slowly as a snail.' Which figure of speech is this?
mcqs.why: The notes call this a simile because the car's slowness is compared using 'as' with a snail, a famously slow creature.

mcqs.q: 'The leaves waved goodbye as they fell from the tree.' Which figure of speech is this?
mcqs.why: The notes identify personification here, because the leaves are given the human action of waving goodbye as they fall.

mcqs.q: 'The alarm clock screamed at me.' Which figure of speech is this?
mcqs.why: The notes call this personification, since the alarm clock is given the human action of screaming at the speaker.

mcqs.q: 'His temper was a volcano, ready to erupt.' Which figure of speech is this?
mcqs.why: The notes identify a metaphor: a direct comparison without 'as' or 'like', where temper is stated to be a volcano.

mcqs.q: 'Her laughter was a sweet symphony.' Which figure of speech is this?
mcqs.why: The notes identify this as a metaphor, a direct comparison in which laughter is stated to be a sweet symphony.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, a simile makes its comparison using which words?
mcqs.why: The notes explain each simile as a comparison using 'as', as in water as cold as ice and a car as slow as a snail.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, how is a metaphor different from a simile?
options: It is a direct comparison without 'as' or 'like'
It gives human actions to objects
It must use the word 'as' twice
mcqs.why: The notes define the metaphors as direct comparisons without 'as'/'like', such as temper being a volcano.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, what happens in personification?
options: Two unlike things are compared using 'as'
A non-human thing is given a human action
A direct comparison is made without 'like'
mcqs.why: The notes explain personification by examples: leaves given the human action of waving, and a clock given the action of screaming.

mcqs.q: Which of the following sentences from the notes is a metaphor?
options: The water was as cold as ice
The leaves waved goodbye as they fell
His temper was a volcano, ready to erupt
The car was moving as slowly as a snail
mcqs.why: Of the listed sentences, only 'His temper was a volcano' is a direct comparison without 'as'/'like', which the notes label a metaphor.

lessons.title: Grammar Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar A

1. to (infinitive of purpose: We go to the garden to plant trees). 2. but (contrast: He studied hard but he failed in the exams). 3. so (result: It was hot outside, so we went back to our homes). 4. but (contrast: She was tired but she did not give up the work). 5. both...and (correlative: She is both intelligent and hardworking). 6. Neither...nor (correlative: Neither the manager nor the employees knew about the change). 7. either...or (correlative: You can either read the book or watch the movie). 8. more...than (comparison: The dish was more delicious than it looked).

Grammar B

Rewrite the given sentences by adding conjunctions to them: 1. You can have ice cream for dessert. You can have cake for dessert. 2. He was tired. He continued to work. 3. They didn't have enough money. They couldn't buy the tickets. 4. You should wear a coat. It is cold outside. 5. The restaurant serves delicious food. The restaurant has great service. 1. You can have either ice cream or cake for dessert. 2. He was tired, but he continued to work. 3. They didn't have enough money, so they couldn't buy the tickets. 4. You should wear a coat because it is cold outside. 5. The restaurant serves delicious food, and it has great service.

Grammar C

Once, a boy named Ali wanted to build a treehouse, but he had no wood and no tools. First, he asked his neighbours for help; moreover, he saved his pocket money for nails. Although the work was hard, he did not give up, because his friends encouraged him. Meanwhile, his sister drew a plan, and Ali followed it carefully. Finally, the treehouse stood complete; therefore, the whole street celebrated, and Ali learned that patience and teamwork turn small beginnings into great results.

mcqs.q: 'We go to the garden to plant trees.' What is the function of 'to' in 'to plant'?
options: It shows contrast between two actions
It is an infinitive of purpose
mcqs.why: The grammar notes label 'to plant' an infinitive of purpose: it tells why we go to the garden, namely to plant trees.

mcqs.q: 'He studied hard but he failed in the exams.' What does 'but' show?
mcqs.why: The notes mark 'but' as showing contrast here, because failing contrasts with studying hard for the examinations.

mcqs.q: 'It was hot outside, so we went back to our homes.' What does 'so' show?
mcqs.why: The notes label 'so' as showing result: going back home was the result of the heat outside.

mcqs.q: 'She is both intelligent and hardworking.' Which conjunction pair is used?
mcqs.why: The notes identify 'both...and' as the correlative pair in this sentence, joining intelligent and hardworking.

mcqs.q: 'Neither the manager nor the employees knew about the change.' Which pair is used?
mcqs.why: The notes give this sentence as the example of the correlative pair 'Neither...nor' joining manager and employees.

mcqs.q: 'You can either read the book or watch the movie.' Which pair offers the choice?
mcqs.why: The notes identify 'either...or' as the correlative pair presenting a choice between reading the book and watching the movie.

mcqs.q: 'The dish was more delicious than it looked.' Which conjunction structure is used?
mcqs.why: The notes label 'more...than' as a comparison structure, comparing how delicious the dish was with how it looked.

mcqs.q: How are these two sentences joined in the notes? 'He was tired. He continued to work.'
options: He was tired, so he continued to work
He was tired, but he continued to work
He was tired because he continued to work
He was tired, and he continued to work, so he rested

options: They didn't have enough money, but they couldn't buy the tickets
They didn't have enough money, so they couldn't buy the tickets
They didn't have enough money although they couldn't buy the tickets
They didn't have enough money, neither could they buy the tickets

options: He gave up building the treehouse

lessons.title: Speaking and Listening
lessons.notes_html:
Oral Communication Skills A

Excessive screen time affects mental health in several ways: it disturbs sleep (bright screens late at night), reduces physical activity and outdoor play, increases comparison and anxiety through social media, and shortens attention. However, screens are not purely harmful: used in limits, they support learning, connection and creativity. The balanced conclusion, echoing the poem 'If' (self-control, not being mastered by anything), is to set limits — fixed screen hours, no phones at meals or bedtime, and regular breaks for sports, reading and family time — so that technology serves us rather than ruling us.

Oral Communication Skills B

Read the following dialogue and practise it with your friends by taking turns. (Dialogue between Kiran and Zaaraa about joining the gardening club.) Summarize the dialogue. SUMMARY FOR PRACTICE: Kiran invites Zaaraa to join the gardening club; Zaaraa at first thinks gardening is boring and only about planting flowers and vegetables. Kiran explains that gardening improves air quality (plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen), reduces stress and promotes relaxation by connecting us with nature away from screens, and lets us grow our own healthier food. Zaaraa is convinced, decides to try gardening at home, and agrees to join the club, noting that sharing produce is also a way to give back to the community. Practice note: read it in pairs, taking turns as Kiran and Zaaraa, with natural intonation for questions and exclamations.

Oral Communication Skills C

'If the road is long and steep, / And the mountain seems too high, / Do not stop, do not sleep — / Keep your goal before your eye. / Step by step the climber goes, / Though the wind is cold and strong; / Every seed the gardener sows / Grows to flower before too long.' Theme: patience, steady effort and hope — the same spirit as Kipling's 'If'. Recitation feedback points: clear pronunciation, suitable pace, pauses at line ends, and feeling in the voice for the hopeful closing lines.

lessons.title: Writing Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills A

If you can dream without letting dreams control you, and think without letting thoughts become your only goal; if you can face both great success and terrible failure and treat both as deceivers, exactly alike; if you can endure hearing your own true words twisted by dishonest men into a trap for the foolish, or see the work of your lifetime destroyed, and yet bend down and rebuild it with poor, worn tools. — Third stanza: If you can gather all your gains into one pile and gamble them on a single throw, and lose everything, and begin again from the very start without ever mentioning your loss; if you can drive your heart, nerves and muscles to keep working for you long after their strength is gone, and simply hold on when nothing remains inside you except your willpower commanding you to hold on.

Writing Skills B

Write the summary of the poem 'If'. SUMMARY: Rudyard Kipling's poem 'If' is addressed by a father to his son as a guide to becoming a man. It lists the qualities of a mature, balanced character: keep your head when others lose theirs and blame you; trust yourself while allowing for others' doubts; wait patiently; do not answer lies with lies or hatred with hatred; dream and think without being ruled by dreams or thoughts; treat Triumph and Disaster as equal impostors; endure twisted truths and rebuild broken work with worn-out tools; risk all, lose, and start again without complaint; force heart, nerve and sinew to serve long after they are spent, holding on by pure will; keep virtue among crowds and the common touch among kings; let neither foes nor friends hurt you; and fill every minute with purposeful effort. The reward, the poem promises, is the Earth and everything in it — and, more importantly, manhood itself.

By a father to his son as a guide to becoming a man

mcqs.why: Writing A paraphrases Triumph and Disaster as facing both great success and terrible failure and treating both as deceivers, exactly alike.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase, who twists your true words into a trap for the foolish?
mcqs.why: The paraphrase says you must endure hearing your own true words twisted by dishonest men into a trap for the foolish.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase, with what must broken work be rebuilt?
mcqs.why: Writing A says that when the work of your lifetime is destroyed, you bend down and rebuild it with poor, worn tools.

mcqs.why: The third stanza paraphrase says: gather all gains, gamble them on a single throw, lose, and begin again without ever mentioning the loss.

chapters.title: Unit 8: The Impact of Globalisation on Culture and Economy

lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

1. Globalisation is the process by which countries, economies and cultures become interconnected and interdependent through increased communication, trade and exchange of ideas — the integration of markets, technologies and policies into a more connected world. 2. It influences a country's economy through trade (new markets for exports like Pakistani textiles, rice and sports goods; access to imports) and investment (foreign companies and CPEC bringing capital, technology and jobs), and its culture through exchange of ideas, fashions, foods, media and languages. 3. Daily-life examples: wearing clothes and eating foods from other countries, watching foreign TV shows and games, using social media to talk to people abroad, learning a language through an app, and buying imported goods in local shops.

While-reading

Digital globalisation refers to the part of globalisation driven by the internet and digital tools: people can access information from around the world instantly, communicate across the globe through social media, messaging apps and video conferencing, collaborate internationally in education, business, science and arts, and create and share content reflecting their own cultures. It has expanded access to education through online courses, webinars and virtual classrooms, and transformed media and communication — while also posing challenges of cultural homogenisation, misinformation and inequality.

While-reading

Globalisation facilitates labour mobility by increasing the demand for skilled labour to manage and operate advanced technologies and systems, which can lead to higher wages and better job prospects for skilled workers. Advances in technology, transportation and communication make it easier for people and goods to move across borders, and multinational companies setting up operations in Pakistan create jobs in information technology, telecommunication and manufacturing — so workers can move, physically and professionally, towards better-paying, skilled work.

While-reading

Globalisation contributes to cultural exchange by letting people from different cultures interact and share their daily lives: social media platforms (Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, TikTok) show how people in other countries live, celebrate holidays and face challenges, promoting empathy and understanding. TV shows, documentaries and video games from various countries are easily accessible; language apps and online dictionaries help students learn new languages and understand other literatures and values; and exposure to global fashion trends and international cuisines diversifies local tastes. Through this exchange, Pakistanis are exposed to different cultures, ideas and lifestyles, which can be enriching and teach appreciation of diversity.

While-reading

Digital globalisation has expanded access to education through online courses, webinars and virtual classrooms, so students can learn about different cultures and subjects from international educators. Students can learn about different cultures, traditions and histories through websites, videos and online articles, and digital tools like language learning apps and online dictionaries make it easier to learn new languages. Digital platforms also allow individuals and communities to create and share content reflecting their own cultures, traditions and stories, preserving and promoting local cultures globally.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Globalisation is the process by which countries, economies and cultures become interconnected and interdependent through increased communication, trade and exchange of ideas, integrating markets, technologies and policies. It promotes economic growth by opening new markets for exports (Pakistan exports textiles, rice and sports goods worldwide, boosting the economy and creating jobs), by attracting foreign investment (foreign companies and CPEC bring capital and technology that improve industries), by expanding industries through access to larger markets, and by creating new jobs, especially in information technology, telecommunication and manufacturing, often with better pay and conditions.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

On the trade front, globalisation opens international markets for Pakistani exports like textiles and agricultural products, while also providing access to a wide range of imported goods that benefit consumers and industries. On the investment side, foreign direct investment, especially through CPEC, brings crucial capital, technology and job opportunities, contributing to infrastructure development and economic growth. Foreign companies have also invested in Pakistan, bringing capital and technology that have improved our industries.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Globalisation has created new job opportunities especially in information technology, telecommunication and manufacturing, as many multinational companies have set up operations in Pakistan. These jobs often offer better pay and working conditions than local companies. It also increases demand for skilled labour to manage advanced technologies and systems, leading to higher wages and better prospects for skilled workers, and it creates work in export industries (textiles, rice, sports goods) and in digital fields such as e-commerce and online content.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Cultural exchange is the sharing of ideas, lifestyles, traditions and daily life between people of different cultures — through social media, TV shows, games, language learning, fashion and food. It benefits people by broadening their understanding of the world, promoting cultural awareness, empathy and understanding, and helping them learn about and appreciate diversity. For students especially, it teaches different perspectives, traditions and histories, and deepens understanding of other literatures and values.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The concern is erosion: as people adopt global trends, some fear that Pakistan's unique cultural practices, languages and heritage might be overshadowed. Related concerns are cultural homogenisation (things becoming uniform or similar worldwide), misinformation, and inequality (the digital divide). The unit's answer is balance: embrace global influences while preserving our own cultural identity, by promoting digital literacy, supporting local content, ensuring ethical standards and bridging the digital divide.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Digital globalisation has made it possible for people to access information from around the world instantly. Students can learn about different cultures, traditions and histories through websites, videos and online articles; digital tools like language learning apps and online dictionaries make learning new languages easier; and online courses, webinars and virtual classrooms let students learn subjects from international educators. This access broadens their understanding of the world and promotes cultural awareness.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Learning about diverse perspectives broadens students' understanding of the world, promotes cultural awareness, empathy and understanding, and helps them appreciate diversity. It deepens their grasp of other literatures, values and cultural aspects, teaches them how people in other countries live, celebrate and face challenges, and — as the unit's conclusion stresses — helps young students think critically about how they can contribute to a global society while staying true to their roots.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Understanding globalisation helps young students appreciate the complexities of the world and think critically about their own role: they can use its opportunities (trade, technology, education, cultural exchange) while guarding Pakistan's cultural identity and economic stability. By finding this balance — embracing global influences without losing their roots — they can contribute as skilled workers, entrepreneurs and informed citizens to a country that benefits from globalisation rather than being overwhelmed by it.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Enhanced connectivity and interdependence. — what is globalisation based on the text.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

By opening up international markets for exports. — how does globalisation primarily impact Pakistan's economy, according to the text.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

By facilitating easier language learning. — how do digital tools primarily impact students, according to the text.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Erosion of traditional Pakistani culture. — according to the text, what is a potential concern regarding impact of globalisation on the Pakistani culture.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

By enabling instant global communication. — how have digital platforms primarily contributed to globalisation, according to the text.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Promoting digital literacy and supporting local content. — what are the strategies to harness the positive aspects of digital globalisation while mitigating its negative effects.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Finding a balance between benefiting from globalisation and maintaining its unique cultural identity and economic stability. — what is the key challenge for Pakistan in managing the effects of globalisation.

lessons.title: Grammar Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar A

Read the given paragraph carefully and identify the subject, verb, and object in each sentence. Underline the subjects once, the verbs twice, and circle the objects. Paragraph: 'Yesterday, Zaaraa and her friends visited the new museum in town. They explored various exhibits and learned about ancient civilizations. The tour guide explained the history of each artifact in great detail. Afterward, Zaaraa bought a souvenir from the gift shop. Her friends admired the beautiful paintings and sculptures on display. Everyone enjoyed the visit and promised to return soon.' 1. Subject: Zaaraa and her friends. Verb: visited. Object: the new museum. 2. Subject: They. Verbs: explored, learned. Objects: various exhibits (of 'explored'); about ancient civilizations (prepositional phrase after 'learned' — no direct object). 3. Subject: The tour guide. Verb: explained. Object: the history of each artifact. 4. Subject: Zaaraa. Verb: bought. Object: a souvenir. 5. Subject: Her friends. Verb: admired. Object: the beautiful paintings and sculptures. 6. Subject: Everyone. Verbs: enjoyed, promised. Object: the visit (of 'enjoyed'); to return (infinitive object of 'promised').

Grammar B

Identify the complex sentences within the paragraph and underline the subordinate clauses. Paragraph: 'I woke up early this morning because the sunlight was streaming through my window. After rubbing the sleep from my eyes, I decided to go for a jogging in the park nearby. Despite the chilly breeze, I enjoyed the fresh air and the sound of birds chirping in the trees. While running, I saw my friend Zaaraa, who waved and joined me for a few laps around the park. Because we both love exercising outdoors, we often meet up for morning runs. After our jog, we sat on a bench and talked about our plans for the weekend. Although it was still early, the park was bustling with people, and children were playing on the playground equipments. Finally, we said goodbye, and promised to meet again.' Complex sentences (one independent clause + at least one dependent clause): 1. 'I woke up early this morning because the sunlight was streaming through my window.' Subordinate clause: because the sunlight was streaming through my window. Independent: I woke up early this morning. 2. 'While running, I saw my friend Zaaraa, who waved and joined me for a few laps around the park.' Subordinate clause: who waved and joined me for a few laps (relative clause describing Zaaraa). ('While running' is a participial phrase, not a clause.) 3. 'Because we both love exercising outdoors, we often meet up for morning runs.' Subordinate clause: Because we both love exercising outdoors. Independent: we often meet up for morning runs. 4. 'Although it was still early, the park was bustling with people.' Subordinate clause: Although it was still early. Independent: the park was bustling with people. Notes: 'After rubbing the sleep from my eyes' and 'After our jog' are phrases, not clauses; 'Despite the chilly breeze' is a prepositional phrase; the remaining sentences are simple or compound, not complex.

Grammar C

1. Because it was raining, we stayed indoors. (Dependent: Because it was raining. Independent: we stayed indoors.) 2. When the bell rang, the students left the classroom. (Dependent: When the bell rang. Independent: the students left the classroom.) 3. I will visit my grandmother if I finish my homework early. (Independent: I will visit my grandmother. Dependent: if I finish my homework early.) 4. Although globalisation brings opportunities, it also poses challenges. (Dependent: Although globalisation brings opportunities. Independent: it also poses challenges.) 5. She bought the book that her teacher had recommended. (Independent: She bought the book. Dependent: that her teacher had recommended.)

Oral Communication Skills A

My favourite hobby is reading, because it opens new worlds, improves my vocabulary and relaxes my mind. Yes, it is good to have a hobby: it fills free time usefully, develops skills and reduces stress. My family has six members: my parents, my grandmother, my elder brother, my younger sister and me. We celebrate special occasions together — on Eid we wear new clothes, visit relatives, share sweets and give Eidi to the children. My school is [school name]. My favourite teacher is my English teacher, because she explains clearly, encourages every student, and makes lessons interesting with stories and discussions.

Oral Communication Skills B

Digital globalisation has changed my understanding of other cultures completely. Before, other countries felt distant; now, through videos, social media and online articles, I see how people in other countries live, celebrate and face challenges, and I feel empathy for them. I have learned words of another language through an app, tasted international foods, and watched documentaries from other countries. At the same time, I have learned to be careful: not everything online is true, so I check information before believing it. Digital globalisation has made the world smaller, but it has also made me value my own Pakistani culture more, because I now understand both what we share with others and what makes us unique.

Writing Skills A

Title: Renewable Energy: Promise and Problems. Renewable energy sources like solar, wind and hydroelectric power are increasingly vital against climate change, being sustainable and cleaner than fossil fuels. Governments and companies are investing heavily in them to cut carbon emissions, but high initial costs and the need for better energy storage still challenge a reliable transition.

Writing Skills A

Title: Nature: Our Life and Our Duty. Nature, in its forests, rivers, oceans and mountains, gives us beauty, inspiration and the essentials of life — clean air, fresh water and fertile soil — and spending time in it calms the mind and reduces stress. We must therefore protect it by reducing pollution, conserving habitats and practising sustainability, so its wonders remain for future generations.

Writing Skills A

Title: Education: The Cornerstone of Progress. Education equips individuals with knowledge, skills and critical thinking, qualifies them for employment, and thereby fosters economic growth and reduces poverty. It also promotes tolerance, empathy and cooperation for inclusive communities, and empowers people to make informed decisions, pursue goals and drive innovation and cultural enrichment.

Writing Skills A

Title: Healthy Eating for a Better Life. A balanced diet of fruits, vegetables, whole grains and lean proteins supplies the nutrients, vitamins and antioxidants needed for energy, immunity and a healthy metabolism. Poor choices — excess sugar, salt and unhealthy fats — cause obesity, diabetes, heart disease and other illnesses, so healthy eating improves both physical health and mental and emotional stability.
