chapters.title: Unit 9: Quality Education: A Key to Success

lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

1. Quality education is education that equips learners with the knowledge, skills, values and attitudes necessary to thrive in a rapidly changing world — a holistic approach that goes beyond enrolment to real learning, including literacy, numeracy, digital literacy and vocational skills, delivered by trained teachers through updated curricula. 2. It is important because it drives economic growth, reduces poverty, promotes gender equality and protects the environment; in Pakistan, where a large portion of the population is young, investing in education can unlock the potential of millions and drive the country towards a prosperous, sustainable future. It is also SDG 4 and a fundamental human right.

While-reading

Quality education empowers individuals by enabling them to realize their full potential and participate actively in social, economic and political spheres. It equips them with essential skills such as literacy, numeracy and digital literacy, laying the foundation for lifelong learning and socio-economic advancement. Educated individuals are more likely to engage in community development, advocate for social justice and contribute to sustainable development; and education is crucial for advancing gender equality by empowering women with knowledge, confidence and opportunities for leadership and economic independence.

While-reading

Education provides literacy, numeracy, digital literacy and vocational skills, which are crucial for enhancing employability, securing better jobs and promoting economic independence, thereby reducing income inequality. Subjects like mathematics, science and technology develop critical thinking and problem-solving abilities in high demand in technology, healthcare and engineering, reducing unemployment and underemployment. By equipping marginalized populations, education acts as a leveller providing equal opportunities regardless of background, gender or ethnicity, and so breaks the cycle of poverty and fosters inclusive growth.

While-reading

STEM stands for Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics. Emphasizing STEM in education equips students with the technical skills necessary for innovation, fosters curiosity and a problem-solving mindset, and drives technological advancements and scientific discoveries.

While-reading

Outdated curricula and pedagogical approaches that fail to equip learners with the skills demanded by the rapidly changing global landscape; shortage of teachers, low salaries and inadequate training, which undermine learning outcomes; and disparities in access, including education in emergencies. The unit's remedy is investment in teachers' professional development and support — professional development programmes, fair salaries and supportive working environments to attract and retain qualified teachers — plus curriculum reform and equitable access.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Quality education is defined as essential for sustainable development: it helps individuals gain the knowledge, skills and values necessary for productive and fulfilling lives, through a holistic approach that equips learners with the knowledge, skills, values and attitudes necessary to thrive in a rapidly changing world. Sustainable development itself, as defined by the United Nations, aims to meet the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Name three benefits of quality education mentioned in the essay. Three benefits: (1) Economic growth — it equips individuals with workforce skills, reduces unemployment and underemployment, and drives innovation and productivity. (2) Reduction of poverty — it acts as a leveller, giving marginalized populations equal opportunities and breaking the cycle of poverty. (3) Gender equality — it empowers women with knowledge, confidence and opportunities for leadership and economic independence. (Other benefits named: environmental protection, social cohesion, better health outcomes, and innovation.)

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Human capital is the knowledge, skills and health that individuals accumulate over their lives, which enables them to contribute effectively to economic growth and development. Quality education enhances human capital by ensuring individuals have the competencies to thrive in a rapidly evolving global economy. A well-educated population drives innovation and productivity, reduces unemployment, and — as an investment in human capital — becomes a pathway to sustainable development, social equity and a more prosperous future for all.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Describe the role of education in reducing inequality and poverty. Education serves as a leveller, providing equal opportunities for all regardless of socio-economic background, gender or ethnicity. By equipping marginalized populations with education, it helps break the cycle of poverty and fosters inclusive growth. Skills (literacy, numeracy, digital literacy, vocational skills) improve employability and economic independence, reducing income inequality; and investing in quality education is presented not just as investment in human capital but as a pathway to social equity and a more prosperous future.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Quality education teaches students about different cultures, religions and perspectives, fostering mutual respect and understanding. Providing equitable access for all, regardless of background, bridges social divides; inclusive education promotes equality and unity, reducing social tensions; schools serve as community hubs where diverse groups come together, fostering belonging and shared purpose. Education also encourages critical thinking about root causes of conflict, cultivates empathy, and enables individuals to engage constructively in democratic processes and resolve conflicts peacefully — promoting a culture of peace.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Quality education fuels innovation and creativity, driving technological advancements and fostering entrepreneurship. By fostering entrepreneurship and innovation, education creates economic opportunities and lifts individuals and communities out of poverty. Entrepreneurial skills — problem-solving, creativity, initiative — turn students into job creators rather than only job seekers, which increases employment, productivity and prosperity, just as the unit's earlier discussion of women's entrepreneurship showed businesses creating jobs for others.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) education equips students with the technical skills necessary for innovation, fosters curiosity and a problem-solving mindset, and is crucial for technological advancements and scientific discoveries. Higher education institutions then play a pivotal role in research and development, providing resources and environment for students and faculty to conduct research leading to new inventions, technologies and methodologies. Together, STEM schooling and university research form the pipeline of innovation.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

In my school, quality could be improved by updating the library with new books and computers, arranging teacher training workshops in modern teaching techniques, and reducing overcrowded classes so teachers can help every student. In my community, we could start evening study circles and a book bank for children who cannot afford textbooks, and invite educated volunteers to tutor younger students. At home, parents can support learning by giving children a quiet study corner and regular reading time. These steps match the unit's remedies: teacher development, curriculum reform, resources and equitable access.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

By focusing economic growth, reducing poverty, and gender equality. — how does quality education contribute to sustainable development.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Focus on sports and entertainment. — which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of quality education in the text.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Mathematics, science, and technology. — which subjects are highlighted as important for developing critical thinking and problem-solving abilities.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Literacy, numeracy, and digital literacy. — what essential skills does education provide that lay the foundation for lifelong learning and socio-economic advancement.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

By encouraging critical thinking. — how does education help in understanding conflicts.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Strengthens communities. — what broader impact does education have on society.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Technical skills for innovation. — what skills does emphasising STEM education aim to develop in students.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

They provide resources and environment for research. — what role do the higher education institutions play in research and development (R&D).

Reading and Critical Thinking C

Provide examples to explain the relationship between these goals and education. Two supporting goals: Goal 1 — No Poverty, and Goal 3 — Good Health and Well-being (Goal 5 — Gender Equality is another strong choice). How they support Goal 4: (1) No Poverty — when families escape poverty, children are not forced to work instead of attending school, and families can afford books, uniforms and fees; poverty reduction therefore raises enrolment and attendance, the first condition of quality education. (2) Good Health and Well-being — healthy children learn better: nutrition, clean water and healthcare reduce absenteeism and improve concentration, while school health programmes (meals, hygiene awareness) directly raise learning outcomes. Example: a village where a poverty-alleviation programme and a school meals programme run together sees both higher attendance and better results — proving that progress on Goals 1 and 3 makes Goal 4 achievable.

Reading and Critical Thinking D

Provide specific examples from the text to support your analysis. Facts and details: The writer presents the reforms through direct observation and quoted voices — newly renovated classrooms with colourful posters and modern learning tools; teacher Ms. Kiran saying the training workshops empowered teachers to use modern techniques after relying on outdated methods; student Zaaraa loving the new books with pictures and activities; and senior teacher Mr. Zeeshaan warning that rural schools still struggle with overcrowded classrooms and limited technology. Tone: hopeful but balanced — warm and optimistic about urban improvements ('excited chatter', 'positive impact'), yet honest about remaining gaps ('not everything was perfect', 'there's still a long way to go'). Personal perspective: as an on-the-spot eyewitness, the writer's first-person account ('As I stood at the school gate...', 'I walked through...', 'I also spoke with...') makes the reforms feel real and human rather than abstract; but the perspective is limited to one urban school on one day, so the account cannot prove that rural schools have improved — a limit the writer himself acknowledges through Mr. Zeeshaan's voice.

Reading and Critical Thinking E

Read paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 10 of the unit carefully. Highlight the impactful words and phrases. Paragraph 1 — impactful words/phrases: 'essential for the sustainable development', 'knowledge, skills, and values', 'holistic approach', 'rapidly changing world', 'meet the needs of the present without compromising... future generations', 'unlock the potential of millions'. Paragraph 2 — 'essential for economic growth', 'critical thinking and problem-solving', 'high demand', 'reduce unemployment and underemployment', 'drive innovation and productivity'. Paragraph 3 — 'powerful tool for empowerment', 'realize their full potential', 'literacy, numeracy, and digital literacy', 'lifelong learning', 'advocate for social justice', 'gender equality', 'leadership and economic independence'. Paragraph 10 — 'fuels innovation and creativity', 'driving technological advancements', 'lift individuals and communities out of poverty', 'informed decisions about their health', 'strengthens communities and societies'.

Grammar A

); 'of Greenfield' (in 'the quiet village of Greenfield' — which village?); 'near the stream' (describes the old oak tree — which tree?). Prepositional phrases (preposition + complement): 'In the quiet village of Greenfield', 'with her grandmother', 'to the nearby forest', 'in search of flowers', 'under the old oak tree', 'near the stream', 'Despite the early hour', 'of energy and enthusiasm'. Adverbial phrases (describe a verb — how/when/where): 'Every morning' (when she walked); 'to the nearby forest' (where she walked — also prepositional in form); 'in search of flowers' (why she walked); 'always' is a single adverb, while 'full of energy and enthusiasm' describes the girl (adjectival). Note: several phrases do double duty — 'in search of flowers' is prepositional in form and adverbial in function (purpose).

Grammar B

1. The children played happily in the school playground in the evening. (adverbial: happily, in the school playground, in the evening) 2. He completed the task with great care before the deadline. (adverbial: with great care, before the deadline) 3. They went on vacation to the northern mountains during the summer holidays. (adverbial/prepositional: to the northern mountains, during the summer holidays) 4. The teacher explained the math problem with simple examples on the whiteboard. (adverbial: with simple examples, on the whiteboard) 5. They attended the wedding in their new clothes at the community hall. (adjectival: in their new clothes; adverbial: at the community hall) 6. lessons.title: Writing Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills A

'Little Women' by Louisa May Alcott (retold by John Escott) is a classic family novel set in America during the Civil War, following the four March sisters — responsible Meg, spirited Jo, gentle Beth and artistic Amy — and their mother Marmee while their father is away at war. The plot follows the sisters through everyday trials and joys: their poverty at Christmas, Jo's struggle with her temper, Amy's longing for pretty things, Beth's quiet kindness, and their gradual growth into young women who learn responsibility, generosity and independence. Jo stands out: hot-tempered and ambitious, she dreams of becoming a writer, sacrifices her beautiful hair to help the family, and slowly learns patience and self-control; Amy, once vain and childish, matures into a graceful, thoughtful young woman. The themes are family love, personal growth and independence — the sisters learn that true wealth is love and character, not money. Alcott's style is warm, descriptive and easy to read, with dialogue that makes each sister feel real and scenes (the Christmas morning without presents, the sisters' plays and picnics) that bring the home to life. I enjoyed the book most for Jo's spirit and the family's kindness, though the pace is slow in places. I recommend 'Little Women' to readers aged 11 and above, especially anyone who loves family stories and strong, growing characters.

Writing Skills B

'The Jungle Book' by Rudyard Kipling is a collection of adventure stories set in the jungles of India, centred on Mowgli, a boy raised by wolves. The plot follows Mowgli's life among the animals — his teachers Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther, his enemy the tiger Shere Khan, and his eventual return to the world of men — as he learns the Law of the Jungle and grows from a helpless child into a brave young man. Mowgli's character shows courage, loyalty and curiosity, but also the challenge of belonging to two worlds. The themes are belonging, the laws of nature, friendship and growing up. Kipling's style is vivid and musical, with songs and rhythmic prose that make the jungle feel alive, though some passages use old-fashioned language. I enjoyed the animal characters most, especially Baloo's wisdom and humour. I recommend 'The Jungle Book' to young readers who love adventure, animals and stories about finding one's place in the world.

lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

L (Learned) — The snow leopard lives up to 5,500 metres in the Himalayas, Karakoram and Hindu Kush, is shy and solitary, and hunts markhor, ibex and wild sheep; the markhor lives up to 3,600 metres in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Balochistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir, eats grasses, shrubs and leaves, has corkscrew horns up to 1.5 metres, and its name means 'snake-eater' in Persian. Both are threatened by poaching, habitat destruction and climate change, but trophy hunting programmes, herder compensation and the work of the Snow Leopard Foundation and WWF-Pakistan are helping their numbers recover.

While-reading

Snow leopards are rarely seen because they are shy and solitary, avoiding human contact whenever possible, and because they live in some of the most remote, high-altitude areas of the world — roaming at altitudes as high as 5,500 metres — where their thick, spotted coat blends perfectly with the rocky mountains. Their elusiveness is why they are called the 'Ghost of the Mountains'.

While-reading

The markhor is a herbivore, feeding on grasses, shrubs and leaves. Living at altitudes of up to 3,600 metres, mark Hors are often seen perched on narrow ledges, grazing on vegetation.

While-reading

Conservation efforts have reduced human-leopard conflict: by compensating herders who lose livestock due to snow leopard attacks and raising awareness of the species' importance, conservationists have reduced the killings of these endangered cats, and an improvement in snow leopard numbers has been seen. Community trophy hunting programmes and the work of the Snow Leopard Foundation and WWF-Pakistan also protect habitats and give local people financial incentives to protect the animals.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The snow leopard, as a top predator, plays a crucial role in maintaining the natural balance: it keeps the populations of herbivores like the markhor in check, ensuring that plant life in these areas remains balanced. Mark Hors, in turn, are critical for maintaining the vegetation of the mountain slopes, preventing overgrazing and soil erosion. The predator-prey relationship is therefore a classic, delicate balance: each species regulates the other, and the health of the whole mountain ecosystem depends on both.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Snow leopard adaptations: thick, spotted coat and dense fur for cold and camouflage; piercing blue eyes; wide, fur-covered paws to walk on snow without sinking; long tail for balance on narrow ledges; muscular build and agility for hunting in steep terrain. Markhor adaptations: wide hooves to climb cliffs with ease; coat that changes with the seasons (warmth in winter, shedding in summer); living in steep, rocky areas where they can quickly flee predators; and long, corkscrew horns (up to 1.5 metres in males). Both are perfectly fitted to high altitudes — the snow leopard to 5,500 metres, the markhor to 3,600 metres.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Benefits: in Chitral National Park and the Toshi Game Reserve, trophy hunting programmes allow foreign hunters to hunt a limited number of mark Hors under strict regulations; the revenue is used for wildlife conservation and to provide financial incentives for local people to protect the animals, so communities gain income and a reason to guard wildlife rather than poach it. Concerns: even regulated hunting kills animals of an endangered species, and there is a risk that financial gain is prioritised over animal welfare, or that quotas are misused; critics also argue that conservation should not depend on killing. The unit presents the programmes as successful overall, but the ethical tension remains a genuine concern.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

If the snow leopard disappeared, herbivore populations like the markhor would increase, causing overgrazing that damages vegetation and the environment — a ripple effect disturbing other animals and the overall health of the mountain environment. If the markhor disappeared, the snow leopard would lose its primary prey and decline, and the vegetation balance the markhor maintains (preventing overgrazing and soil erosion) would also be disturbed. Without either species, the entire ecosystem would be at risk; protecting them preserves the environment they inhabit.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Poaching, habitat destruction and climate change have reduced populations of both species: mark Hors have been hunted for their valuable horns, while snow leopards have been killed by herders trying to protect their livestock. These activities upset the delicate predator-prey balance — fewer prey weakens predators, fewer predators lets herbivores overgraze — and shrink the habitats both need, pushing both species towards vulnerability despite their adaptations.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The markhor is perfectly adapted to steep, rocky terrain: its wide hooves help it climb cliffs with ease; its coat changes with the seasons, providing warmth in winter and shedding in summer; it lives at altitudes of up to 3,600 metres, often perched on narrow ledges grazing on vegetation, where it can quickly flee predators; and males carry long, twisted, corkscrew-shaped horns up to 1.5 metres. It is found in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Balochistan and parts of Azad Jammu and Kashmir.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

More can be done through school programmes and documentaries about the 'Ghost of the Mountains' and Pakistan's national animal; through community meetings in mountain areas explaining the compensation schemes for herders; through social media campaigns by the Snow Leopard Foundation and WWF-Pakistan showing the animals' beauty and their ecosystem role; through eco-tourism that lets people see the animals without disturbing them; and through stricter enforcement against poaching and habitat destruction, with rewards for communities that protect wildlife. Awareness works best when it combines knowledge (why the balance matters) with incentives (why protecting pays).

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The description changed my understanding from 'two rare animals' to 'two partners in a fragile system'. The vivid details — the snow leopard's spotted coat blending with rock, its fur-covered paws on snow, the markhor's corkscrew horns like coiled snakes — made the animals feel real and magnificent, while the account of threats and conservation showed that their survival depends on human choices. I now understand that saving a predator and its prey is not about choosing one animal, but about preserving the whole mountain ecosystem and Pakistan's natural heritage.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

The population of herbivores like markhor would increase, leading to overgrazing. — what might be the long-term impact on the ecosystem if the snow leopard were to become extinct.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

They generate income for locals and fund wildlife protection efforts. — how do community-based conservation efforts, such as trophy hunting, benefit both wildlife and local people.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Involving local communities in conservation efforts leads to better outcomes. — what lesson can be learned from the successful conservation efforts of the snow leopard and the markhor.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

To keep herbivore populations in check and protect vegetation. — why is it important to maintain the balance between predator and prey in ecosystems like those of the snow leopard and the markhor.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

They may prioritise financial gain over the welfare of animals. — what is one potential drawback of trophy hunting programmes, even when they help conservation efforts.

Reading and Critical Thinking C

Read the following text and put relevant information into the graphic organiser (Cause / Problem / Effect / Solution). Text: There is a serious threat to the snow leopard and the markhor in Pakistan's mountains. Poaching and habitat loss have decreased their numbers. Snow leopards are also killed by herders protecting their livestock. These problems lead to an imbalance in the ecosystem. Without snow leopards, the markhor population can increase, causing overgrazing and damaging the environment. Conservation efforts include trophy hunting programmes that help protect wildlife. Compensation for herders also reduces the killing of snow leopards. These actions aim to save both species and protect the ecosystem. Cause — Poaching, habitat loss, and herders killing snow leopards to protect livestock. Problem — The numbers of snow leopards and mark Hors in Pakistan's mountains have seriously decreased; both species are threatened. Effect — Imbalance in the ecosystem: without snow leopards, the markhor population can increase, causing overgrazing and damaging the environment. Solution — Trophy hunting programmes that fund wildlife protection and give locals incentives to protect animals; compensation for herders who lose livestock, reducing the killing of snow leopards; together these actions aim to save both species and protect the ecosystem.

lessons.title: Speaking and Listening
lessons.notes_html:
Oral Communication Skills A

Present findings and join a whole-class discussion. Main idea — Despite threats, conservation efforts in Pakistan are working, but both species remain vulnerable and continued effort is needed. Supporting details — the Snow Leopard Foundation and WWF-Pakistan work tirelessly; in Chitral National Park and Toshi Game Reserve, communities with the government run trophy hunting programmes whose revenue funds conservation and incentivises locals; compensating herders and raising awareness have reduced snow leopard killings and improved numbers. Whole-class point — success came from involving local people, not excluding them.

Oral Communication Skills B

The Snow Leopard Foundation works in Pakistan's high mountains to protect the ghost of the mountains and its prey. It studies snow leopards, trains local people as trackers and guards, and runs the compensation scheme that pays herders for livestock lost to leopards — so herders no longer need to kill the cats in revenge. Its successes include rising snow leopard numbers in project valleys; its challenges include vast, rugged terrain and the poverty that drives poaching. Its work matters because it restores the balance: with leopards present, markhor numbers stay in check, vegetation recovers, and the whole mountain ecosystem — and the communities that depend on it — stays healthy. WWF-Pakistan plays a similar role, combining science, community programmes and policy advocacy for the same goal.

Oral Communication Skills C

Conservationist: 'The snow leopard and the markhor keep our mountains in balance — lose one, and the whole ecosystem suffers.' Community Member: 'Since the trophy programme began, our village earns money for protecting animals instead of poaching them, and our children see the markhor as a treasure.' Government Official: 'We will expand the compensation scheme for herders and fund more guards for Chitral National Park and Toshi Game Reserve.' Local Entrepreneur: 'Eco-tourism can help too: visitors who come to see the markhor and, with luck, the snow leopard, bring income that depends on the animals staying alive.' Together: 'Protecting predator and prey protects us all.'

Oral Communication Skills D

Half the class argues saving the snow leopard is more important for maintaining balance; the other half argues saving the markhor is equally important due to its role in preventing overgrazing and its cultural significance. For the snow leopard side: As top predator, the leopard regulates the whole system; without it, markhor overgraze and vegetation collapses, harming every species including the markhor. For the markhor side: Without prey, the leopard starves; the markhor also maintains vegetation directly (preventing overgrazing and soil erosion) and is Pakistan's national animal, a cultural symbol whose loss would be a national loss. Synthesis: both sides actually prove the same point — predator and prey can only be saved together, because the balance needs both; conservation must protect habitats, compensate herders and involve communities for both species at once.

Oral Communication Skills E

Words to practise: elusive (ee-LOO-siv), herbivore (HER-bi-vor), conservation (kon-ser-VAY-shun), ecosystem (EE-koh-sis-tem), vulnerable (VUL-ner-uh-bul), magnificent (mag-NIF-i-sent), rugged (RUG-id), predator (PRED-uh-ter). Sentences to practise with rising/falling intonation: 'Often referred to as the Ghost of the Mountains, the snow leopard roams at altitudes as high as 5,500 metres.' (falling, statement) 'Why are snow leopards rarely seen by humans?' (falling, wh-question) 'The markhor, with its impressive corkscrew-shaped horns, is Pakistan's national animal.' (falling, statement). Listening rule: eyes on the text, ears on the teacher's stress and pauses; repeat each sentence aloud after the teacher.

lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills A

The Ghost of the Mountains. In the high-altitude regions of Pakistan, where the peaks of the Himalayas, Karakoram and Hindu Kush touch the sky, lives one of the most elusive animals on the planet: the snow leopard. It is important because, as a top predator, it keeps the mountain ecosystem in balance, and because its beauty makes it a symbol of Pakistan's wild heritage. In appearance, the snow leopard is magnificent: a thick, spotted coat that blends perfectly with rocky mountains, piercing blue eyes, a muscular build, wide fur-covered paws and a long tail. Its adaptations fit its home exactly: the dense fur survives bitter cold, the wide paws walk on snow without sinking, and the long tail balances it on narrow ledges at altitudes up to 5,500 metres. In behaviour, it is shy and solitary, avoiding humans, and it hunts markhor, ibex and wild sheep. Its importance is beyond its beauty: without it, herbivores would overgraze and damage the mountains. Protecting the snow leopard therefore means protecting the whole mountain world it rules so silently.

lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

1. The title 'The Dear Departed' suggests death and mourning — a beloved family member who has died, a funeral, grief, and the settling of the dead person's affairs. 2. The tone turns out to be humorous rather than purely serious, despite the death: the play is a satire in which the 'departed' grandfather is not dead at all, and the comedy comes from the daughters' greed, their mourning clothes, and their panic when he walks in alive. The title itself is ironic — the 'dear departed' is neither dear (his daughters quarrel over his things) nor departed.

While-reading

The living room of the Slater family's house is modest and functional, in the style of an early 20th-century Edwardian home, reflecting the family's middle-class status. It is the play's sole location, creating an intimate, focused environment. The decor is simple and functional, the furniture practical and slightly worn, the lighting soft (lamps or candles) with a warm but slightly dim glow, and the colour palette muted — brown, cream and grey — giving a conservative, somewhat sombre tone, calm with an air of formality typical of the period.

While-reading

A large central dining table covered with a white cloth stands in the middle, surrounded by chairs. To one side there is a sofa for seating, with other simple chairs and a small side table. At the back of the room a staircase leads upstairs; a mantelpiece displays a clock, and there may be a sideboard or cabinet against one wall, with framed photographs hanging on the walls. There is also a door leading outside, positioned to one side.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Their true motivation is material gain, not grief. Mrs. Slater, before the Jordans arrive, hurries Victoria out of coloured clothes into half-mourning so the Slaters 'outshine' the Jordans; she takes her dead father's new slippers for Henry, moves the bureau and the clock downstairs before Elizabeth can claim them, and calls the chest of drawers 'shabby' to justify the swap. Mrs. Jordan arrives in complete new mourning with plumes, boasts about ready-made versus ordered mourning, claims the gold watch was promised to her Jimmy, and later accuses Amelia of robbery only to secure her own share. Both sisters compete over the bureau, the clock, the watch and the insurance money, and both suddenly want Abel to live with them only when he announces a new will leaving everything to whomever he lives with at his death. Their greed drives every action: the mourning is a costume, the tears are performance, and sisterly affection collapses into quarrelling the moment possessions are at stake.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The conflict over possessions is the engine of the whole plot: it opens with Amelia's plan to move the bureau and clock, continues through the sisters' rivalry over the gold watch and the insurance premium, peaks when Abel discovers his bureau and clock downstairs, and resolves with his new-will announcement and marriage plan. It reveals that the characters value things over people: Abel's 'death' is treated as an opportunity to divide 'his bits of things', the announcement in the papers is debated for 'the look of the thing', and both daughters measure love by what they receive. Only Victoria, and finally Abel himself, see the truth — that the family prized the inheritance above the man.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The approach is highly effective because comedy makes the criticism sting without preaching: the audience laughs at the sisters and then recognizes the same materialism in real families. The final twist — Abel marrying Mrs. John Shorrocks and taking his bureau to the Ring-o'-Bells — is the satirist's perfect revenge on greed.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The play demolishes the idea of automatic family unity: the two sisters, who have quarrelled for two years (Elizabeth once said she would not take Abel 'at any price' and had 'enough of you to last a lifetime'), unite only to divide his property, and turn on each other the moment Abel's will is mentioned. It suggests that when material wealth is involved, family ties can become transactional: affection is performed (kisses, tears, mourning clothes) while the real currency is the bureau, the clock, the watch and the insurance money. Abel's verdict — 'neither of you cared to put up with me' — states the play's message: where inheritance rules, love is conditional and unity is a show.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The clock is Abel's handsome clock, which Amelia fetches downstairs because 'our clock's worth nothing and this always appealed to me'. It betrays the theft: when it strikes six, Abel recognizes it — 'Drat me if that isn't my clock too' — and demands to know what has been going on. Symbolically, the clock marks the family's attitude to time: they treat Abel's life as finished (his time is up) and rush to divide his things before the 'proper' mourning period, while the striking clock announces that his time is not over at all. It also symbolizes routine and respectability — the mantelpiece clock as a household prize — and inheritance itself: a valuable, visible object that both sisters covet and that exposes their greed.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Unlike the adults, she does not dress her actions in excuses — she sees the bureau and clock removal for what it is (taking things before the rightful heirs arrive) and she is genuinely glad Abel is alive ('Oh, Grandpa, I'm so glad you're not dead'), while her mother hisses, 'Hold your tongue, Victoria.' Her perspective tells us that the younger generation sees through adult hypocrisy: children notice greed and dishonesty even when adults disguise them as propriety, and Victoria's honesty functions as the play's moral voice.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Hypocrisy is everywhere: Amelia weeps over 'the little trifles that belonged to grandfather' while stealing his bureau and clock; she claims grandpa 'gave it to your mother before he died' when Victoria asks if they are pinching it. Elizabeth arrives in full mourning and kisses Amelia solemnly, then accuses her of robbery ('They sneaked into your room like a thief in the night') while herself claiming the gold watch for Jimmy. Henry wears Abel's slippers and helps move the bureau, then moralizes about delicacy. Both sisters insist they loved their father, yet neither wants him alive: when Abel announces his new will, both suddenly compete to house him — not from love, but for the inheritance. Words say grief and family; actions say greed.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The single living room forces all the characters into one space with no escape: the sisters must perform grief face to face, the bureau swap must be hidden in the same room where the Jordans will sit, and Abel's entrance traps everyone together for the confrontation. The confinement heightens tension and comedy — whispered prompts ('Frederick' / 'Albert'), the bumping of the bureau against the wall, the clock striking six in front of everyone. It suggests that these relationships are themselves confined and airless: the family is locked together by blood and property, unable to be honest or to leave, so politeness and greed collide in a small room that mirrors their narrow, materialistic world.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Houghton builds tension in stages: exposition — Amelia's mourning preparations and the secret plan for the bureau; rising action — the bureau and clock are moved downstairs just before the Jordans knock; complication — the sisters' rivalry over the watch and the possibly unpaid insurance premium raises the stakes; climax — Victoria announces 'Grandpa's getting up', and Abel enters alive in his dressing-gown; revelation — Abel notices his slippers on Henry, his bureau and his clock, and Elizabeth exposes the theft; resolution — Abel's new will and his marriage announcement turn the tables, leaving the sisters with nothing and the bureau itself carried off to the Ring-o'-Bells. Each step peels away another layer of pretence until the true motives — greed on both sides — stand exposed.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The themes remain fully relevant: families today still quarrel over inheritance — houses, jewellery, land, bank accounts — and siblings still compete over a parent's will, sometimes breaking relations for years. Contemporary examples include disputes over a family home after a parent's death, arguments about who keeps a parent's car or ornaments, and even public rows over a celebrity's estate. Social media adds a modern layer: performative grief online (mourning posts) alongside private disputes over property, exactly like the Slaters' mourning clothes versus their bureau theft. The play's warning — that valuing things above people destroys family bonds — applies whenever money enters family love.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A

Find the connotative and denotative meanings of these words: precocious, gallivanting, speck, bureau, impassive, hearth. precocious — Denotative: having developed particular abilities and ways of behaving at a much younger age than usual (Victoria is a precocious girl). Connotative: cheeky, too knowing for a child — Victoria's bluntness embarrasses the adults. — gallivanting — Denotative: to go from place to place enjoying yourself. Connotative: irresponsible wandering, especially improper at a time of mourning (Amelia scolds Victoria for 'gallivanting about in the street' with her grandfather dead upstairs). — speck — Denotative: a very small spot; a small piece of dirt. Enact this one-act play in the class. [Performance notes] PERFORMANCE NOTES: Cast — Mrs. Amelia Slater, Henry Slater, Victoria Slater, Mrs. Elizabeth Jordan, Ben Jordan, Mr. Abel Merryweather. Single set — the Slater living room (table with white cloth, chairs, sofa, mantelpiece with clock, staircase door, front door). Key moments to stage: the bureau move (bumping, whispers, Victoria's questions); the Jordans' entrance in full new mourning (solemn kisses, silent inspection of mourning); the tea-table debate over the newspaper announcement; Victoria's terrified entrance ('Grandpa's getting up'); Abel's entrance in dressing-gown and stockinged feet; the clock striking six; Abel's final announcement at the door. Tone: comic but pointed — play the mourning solemnly and the greed briskly, so the audience laughs and then feels the sting.

Oral Communication Skills D

Humour is the play's weapon: it makes the criticism of greed enjoyable and therefore sharper. Comic devices include irony (mourning a living man), exaggeration (complete new mourning with plumes, the invented dead brother Isaac/Frederick/Albert), incongruity (Ben's chirpy jokes at a 'funeral', the poetic epitaph 'sacred to we'), and the final comic reversal (Abel alive, marrying the pub landlady, and carrying off his own bureau). Without humour, the play would be a grim accusation; with it, the audience laughs at the sisters, recognizes its own materialism, and remembers the moral — that is why satire, not tragedy, is Houghton's chosen form.

Oral Communication Skills E

I can relate to the pressure to 'look right' in front of relatives — like Amelia wanting to outshine Elizabeth in mourning, families sometimes care more about what guests think than about what is true or kind. I have also seen relatives compete over small things after a grandparent's death, such as who keeps a watch or a piece of furniture, and felt, like Victoria, that the quarrel was unworthy of the person who had died. The play taught me that real respect for elders means caring for them while they live — as Abel wished — not performing grief or dividing their things after they are gone.

lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Reading and Critical Thinking A

Yes, the advice in 'If' is deeply relevant today. Self-control when others lose their heads is needed in an age of social-media anger and blame; trusting yourself while allowing for others' doubts is the balance behind critical thinking; not making dreams your master warns against letting ambition or online fame rule your life; treating Triumph and Disaster alike guards against both arrogance in success and despair in failure; and holding on when nothing is left except the Will speaks directly to students facing exams, competition and pressure. The poem's world (Edwardian, 1910) differs from ours, but its virtues — patience, integrity, humility, resilience — are timeless, which is why the poem is still quoted in classrooms and sports teams today.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Globalisation spreads cultural practices through trade, media, migration and digital platforms: social media shows how people in other countries live, celebrate holidays and face challenges; TV shows, documentaries and video games from various countries are easily accessible; language apps and online dictionaries spread languages and literatures; and global fashion trends and international cuisines diversify local tastes. Examples: Pakistani students wearing international fashion brands and eating Chinese, Turkish or Italian food; Eid and Christmas greetings shared worldwide on social media; K-pop, Hollywood films and cricket reaching audiences far beyond their home countries; and Pakistani textiles, music and food becoming known abroad. The exchange enriches, but — as Unit 8 warns — it also risks eroding local traditions unless balance is kept.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Main problems: poaching (mark Hors hunted for valuable horns), habitat destruction, climate change, and snow leopards killed by herders protecting livestock — all reducing both populations and upsetting the predator-prey balance. Solutions implemented: the Snow Leopard Foundation and WWF-Pakistan protection programmes; trophy hunting programmes in Chitral National Park and Toshi Game Reserve (limited hunting under strict regulations, revenue funding conservation and local incentives); and compensation for herders who lose livestock, plus awareness-raising. Effectiveness: the unit reports real improvement in snow leopard numbers and community support, so the solutions are substantially effective; but both species remain vulnerable, so continued habitat protection and anti-poaching enforcement are still needed — the solutions work, but they are not yet complete.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The title suggests a beloved person who has died and is mourned — 'dear' for loved, 'departed' for dead — and points to the play's theme of how families behave around death and inheritance. It is ironic twice over: Abel Merryweather is not departed at all — he is alive upstairs, merely dazed — and he is not truly 'dear' to his daughters, who quarrel over his bureau, clock, watch and insurance money rather than grieving for him. The 'dear departed' of the title is thus a polite fiction the characters perform, while the play exposes the greed beneath the mourning.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Humour is the play's vehicle for serious themes: irony (mourning a living man), exaggeration (full new mourning with plumes; the invented dead brother Isaac/Frederick/Albert), incongruity (Ben's chirpy jokes at a 'funeral'; the epitaph 'sacred to we'), and the final reversal (Abel alive, marrying the pub landlady, carrying off his own bureau). Through laughter, Houghton exposes family conflict (the sisters' quarrel over the will) and hypocrisy (tears performed while property is stolen) without preaching: the audience laughs at the Slaters and Jordans and then recognizes the same materialism in real families. Humour makes the moral memorable — greed looks ridiculous before it looks shameful.

Meaning: extremely important, because it will affect other things. Part of speech: adjective. — population — Pronunciation: /pop-yuh-LAY-shun/ (/ˌpɒpjəˈleɪʃn/). The teacher paid me a compliment on my neat handwriting.

A bad smell from a drain

Foul — to wander; fowl — to wonder
Foul — a bad smell from the drain; fowl — birds such as hens and ducks

Both words mean impossible to read
Respectable describes a family known for honesty, worthy of respect; respectful describes students showing respect towards their teacher
Respectable is a verb and respectful is a noun

The yolk of the egg is yellow and rich.

lessons.title: Grammar Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar A

(because / although / but) 1. or (a choice: the beach or the museum). 2. because (reason: he missed the bus because he woke up late). 3. Until (condition of time: Until you finish your homework, you cannot go outside). 4. nor (correlative: Neither Ali nor his sister wanted to join). 5. but (contrast: She is tired but she kept working until midnight).

Grammar B

Read each sentence carefully and determine whether it is a simple sentence or a complex sentence. Write your answer and explain why it fits that category: 1. The cat sat on the windowsill and watched the birds. 2. Even though it was raining, the children continued to play outside. 3. He finished his homework before dinner. 4. Because she studied hard, Maria passed the exam with flying colours. 5. The sun set behind the mountains. 1. Simple sentence — one independent clause (one subject, 'the cat', with a compound predicate 'sat... and watched...'); no subordinate clause. 2. Complex sentence — independent clause 'the children continued to play outside' + dependent clause 'Even though it was raining'. 3. Simple sentence — one independent clause; 'before dinner' is a prepositional phrase, not a clause. 4. Complex sentence — independent clause 'Maria passed the exam with flying colours' + dependent clause 'Because she studied hard'. 5. Simple sentence — one independent clause, subject 'the sun', verb 'set'.

Grammar C

' 1. Sarah said that she was going to the market. 2. The teacher asked if/whether I had completed my homework. (Question → asked + if/whether; present perfect → past perfect.) 3. Tahir said that he would finish his project by the next day. (will → would; tomorrow → the next day.) 4. She exclaimed with joy that it was a very beautiful painting. 5. Javed asked when they were leaving for the trip. (Question word 'when' kept as the connector; present continuous → past continuous.)

mcqs.q: Which conjunction completes a choice between the beach and the museum, in Grammar A?
mcqs.why: Grammar A gives 'or' for item 1 because it presents a choice: the beach or the museum, unlike 'because' which gives a reason.

mcqs.q: Why is 'because' the correct conjunction for 'he missed the bus ___ he woke up late'?
options: It gives a reason: he missed the bus because he woke up late
mcqs.why: The notes explain item 2 uses 'because' as it gives the reason — he missed the bus because he woke up late — for the action in the main clause.

mcqs.q: Which conjunction begins the time condition '___ you finish your homework, you cannot go outside'?
mcqs.why: Grammar A gives 'Until' as a condition of time: Until you finish your homework, you cannot go outside, so going outside depends on finishing first.

mcqs.q: In 'Neither Ali ___ his sister wanted to join', which conjunction is used?
mcqs.why: The notes give 'nor' as the correlative partner: Neither Ali nor his sister wanted to join, so 'nor' must follow 'neither'.

mcqs.q: Why is 'The cat sat on the windowsill and watched the birds' a simple sentence?
options: It has a dependent clause beginning with 'because'
It has one independent clause with one subject and a compound predicate, and no subordinate clause
It has two subjects and two clauses
It is only a phrase, not a sentence
mcqs.why: Grammar B explains it is a simple sentence: one independent clause, one subject 'the cat', with a compound predicate 'sat... and watched...', and no subordinate clause.

mcqs.q: 'Even though it was raining, the children continued to play outside' is a complex sentence because:
options: 'Before dinner' is a phrase in it
It has an independent clause plus the dependent clause 'Even though it was raining'
It has a compound predicate only
mcqs.why: The notes classify it as complex because it combines the independent clause 'the children continued to play outside' with the dependent clause 'Even though it was raining'.

mcqs.q: Why is 'He finished his homework before dinner' a simple sentence?
options: Because 'before dinner' is a prepositional phrase, not a clause
Because it has a dependent clause
mcqs.why: Grammar B explains this is a simple sentence with one independent clause, since 'before dinner' is a prepositional phrase, not a clause.

mcqs.q: Which is the indirect speech form given for Sarah's statement about the market?
options: Sarah exclaimed that she goes to the market.
Sarah said to me, 'I am going to the market.'
Sarah asked if she was going to the market.
Sarah said that she was going to the market.
mcqs.why: Grammar C gives 'Sarah said that she was going to the market' as the indirect form, with the present continuous backshifted to past continuous.

mcqs.q: In 'The teacher asked if/whether I had completed my homework', what tense change is noted?
options: Present continuous changes to past continuous
Present perfect changes to past perfect, and the question uses asked with if/whether
mcqs.why: The notes explain the question becomes asked plus if/whether, and the present perfect changes to the past perfect in indirect speech.

mcqs.q: How are 'will' and 'tomorrow' changed in Tahir's reported sentence?
options: Will stays will, and tomorrow stays tomorrow
Will becomes would, and tomorrow becomes the next day
Will becomes shall, and tomorrow becomes yesterday
Will becomes would, and tomorrow becomes that night
mcqs.why: Grammar C notes Tahir said he would finish his project by the next day, showing will changes to would and tomorrow changes to the next day in indirect speech.

lessons.title: Speaking and Listening
lessons.notes_html:
Oral Communication Skills A

' Student: 'I am planning to study tonight.' Indirect: The student said that he was planning to study that night. (Rules applied: tense backshift, 'last night' → 'the previous night', 'tonight' → 'that night', 'will' → 'would'.)

Oral Communication Skills B

MODEL ONE-MINUTE SPEECH (SDG 4 — Quality Education): 'Good morning! My SDG is Goal 4: Quality Education. Quality education means every child gets a good education — trained teachers, updated books, safe classrooms and equal chances for girls and boys. It matters because education reduces poverty, creates jobs, promotes equality and helps the environment — it is the key to all the other goals. In Pakistan, millions of children still lack quality schooling, so we must invest in teachers, curricula and access. Let us remember: when we educate one child, we change one future; when we educate all children, we change the world. Thank you!' (Other SDGs can follow the same pattern: name, meaning, why it matters, a Pakistan example, a closing line.)

Oral Communication Skills C

Last summer, on a school trip to the Margalla Hills, our group spotted a family of monkeys on the trail. At first we were excited and moved closer, but our teacher stopped us: wild animals need space, and feeding them harms them. We watched quietly from a distance as the monkeys groomed each other and the babies played — a small, perfect scene of nature undisturbed. That experience taught me what Unit 10 teaches about the snow leopard and the markhor: wildlife survives only when humans respect its space, protect its habitat, and choose observation over interference.

Oral Communication Skills D

Theme — materialism and hypocrisy in family relationships. Message for society — when inheritance and possessions become more important than people, family bonds break: the Slaters and Jordans perform grief while stealing the dead man's bureau and clock, and both daughters refuse to house their father until his new will makes him profitable. For human relationships generally, the play warns that love must be proved while people are alive (Abel: 'neither of you cared to put up with me'), not performed after they are gone; and that respectability — mourning clothes, polite tears, newspaper announcements — can hide selfishness. A healthy society, the play suggests, values people above property.

mcqs.q: What is the indirect form of 'I am planning to study tonight', as given in the notes?
options: The student said that he is planning to study tonight.
The student said that he was planning to study that night.
The student asked if he was planning to study.
The student said to study that night.
mcqs.why: Oral Communication Skills A gives 'The student said that he was planning to study that night', applying tense backshift and changing 'tonight' to 'that night'.

mcqs.why: The rules listed in the notes include tense backshift, 'last night' to 'the previous night', 'tonight' to 'that night', and 'will' to 'would'.

Every child gets a good education — trained teachers, updated books, safe classrooms and equal chances for girls and boys
Education only for children in cities

It replaces all other goals completely
It reduces poverty, creates jobs, promotes equality and helps the environment

Millions of children still lack quality schooling, so we must invest in teachers, curricula and access
Pakistan needs no investment in education

options: Education is only for the rich.
When we educate one child, we change one future; when we educate all children, we change the world.

options: Wild animals need space, and feeding them harms them

options: Trips to hills should be avoided
Wildlife should be fed by visitors
Animals should be kept in classrooms
Wildlife survives only when humans respect its space, protect its habitat and choose observation over interference
mcqs.why: The notes conclude wildlife survives only when humans respect its space, protect its habitat, and choose observation over interference, as Unit 10 teaches about the snow leopard and markhor.

options: Materialism and hypocrisy in family relationships
mcqs.why: Oral Communication Skills D states the theme plainly as materialism and hypocrisy in family relationships, shown by the Slaters and Jordans performing grief while stealing property.

mcqs.why: The notes conclude that a healthy society values people above property, and love must be proved while people are alive, not performed after they are gone.

lessons.title: Writing Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills A

If you can remain calm and in control of yourself at a time when everyone around you is losing their temper and self-control and blaming you for the trouble, then you have the first quality of a mature person.

Writing Skills B

Quality education is the key to success — for individuals and for nations. It is not merely enrolment in a school, but learning that truly equips a person: trained teachers who explain clearly, an engaging curriculum that builds critical thinking, a safe learning environment, and access to technology and resources. Its benefits are wide: it empowers individuals with literacy, numeracy and digital skills; it creates better jobs and reduces poverty; it promotes gender equality and social cohesion; and it strengthens whole communities. Yet challenges remain: lack of resources, overcrowded classrooms, inequality of access, and inadequate teacher training. These can be overcome by investing in teacher development, updating curricula, and ensuring equitable access for every child. In conclusion, improving education improves everything else — if we want a brighter future, we must begin in the classroom.

Writing Skills C

My service to society begins with small, sincere actions in my own surroundings. I keep my street clean, help elderly neighbours with their work, and tutor younger children in my neighbourhood who struggle with their lessons. At school, I take part in cleanliness drives and plantation campaigns, because a green, clean environment benefits everyone. I also obey the law, speak politely to all, and use social media to spread useful information rather than rumours. I believe that serving society does not require wealth or power; it requires a willing heart, honest conduct and regular small deeds, and if every citizen serves in this way, the whole society becomes stronger, kinder and more prosperous.

Remaining calm and in control when everyone around is losing temper and blaming you
mcqs.why: Writing Skills A paraphrases the opening of 'If': remaining calm and in control of yourself while everyone around loses temper and blames you is the first quality of a mature person.

By spreading rumours on social media
mcqs.why: The service essay says the writer keeps his street clean, helps elderly neighbours with their work, and tutors younger children in his neighbourhood who struggle with their lessons.

mcqs.why: The essay states the writer takes part in cleanliness drives and plantation campaigns at school, because a green, clean environment benefits everyone.

options: He never uses it at all
To spread useful information rather than rumours
mcqs.why: Writing Skills C says the writer uses social media to spread useful information rather than rumours, along with obeying the law and speaking politely to all.

options: A willing heart, honest conduct and regular small deeds
mcqs.why: The essay concludes serving society does not require wealth or power; it requires a willing heart, honest conduct and regular small deeds by every citizen.
